entries.title: Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia
entries.summary: Prosecutors say the Berlin marketing executive used her political and military contacts to help a Russian intelligence officer gain access to influential circles and seek information on German defense policy.
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia

Published September 14, 2026last updated September 14, 2026

Prosecutors say the Berlin marketing executive used her political and military contacts to help a Russian intelligence officer gain access to influential circles and seek information on German defense policy.

German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said.

She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.

What is Ilona W. accused of?

Prosecutors say Ilona W. ran a marketing agency in Berlin and also chaired a lobbying association, giving her extensive contacts in military and political circles.

She allegedly had contact with a full-time Russian intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin from at least October 2023.

According to the indictment, she repeatedly supplied him with information about high-profile events and helped arrange access for him, in some cases under a false name.

Prosecutors say the aim was to allow the Russian intelligence officer to build up his own network for intelligence purposes.

What information was she allegedly seeking?

Ilona W. is also accused of attending events herself to identify useful contacts and potential targets.

Prosecutors say she tried to recruit people from Germany's Defense Ministry and the arms industry.

She also allegedly sought information on German defense policy and the defense industry on behalf of her Russian contact, particularly in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine.

The charges were filed last week before the state security division of Berlin's Higher Regional Court.

Germany expelled the suspected Russian intelligence officer linked to the case shortly after W.'s arrest, prompting Moscow to retaliate by expelling a German diplomat.

Edited by Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany news: Foreign minister seeks reset with Hungary
entries.summary: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Hungary as Berlin seeks to rebuild relations with Budapest. Meanwhile, Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Foreign minister seeks reset with Hungary

Published September 14, 2026last updated September 14, 2026

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Hungary as Berlin seeks to rebuild relations with Budapest. Meanwhile, Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says Berlin and Budapest have a lot of diplomatic ground to make up
  • Wadephul says he hopes Hungary's new pro-European government can help rebuild trust
  • Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to 43.5%, its lowest level in 20 years
  • A study blames high construction costs, higher interest rates and housing policy

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, September 14, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Nearly half of German schoolchildren report sleep problems

Nearly half of German schoolchildren report sleep problems

Almost half of schoolchildren in Germany say they regularly have problems sleeping, according to a new survey published by health insurer DAK-Gesundheit.

The survey found that 46% of pupils in grades five to 10 experience sleep problems at least once a week, up from 36% in the 2019/2020 school year.

At the same time, 69% said they felt drained or exhausted at least once a week. Three years ago, the figure was 52%.

Michael Hubmann, president of Germany's professional association of pediatricians, pointed to excessive media use as one factor behind the increase in sleep and exhaustion problems.

"Children and adolescents who use social media until late in the evening or consume disturbing videos triggered by algorithms are being kept from healthy sleep," he said.

DAK chief executive Andreas Storm warned that persistent exhaustion and sleep problems could make it harder for children to learn successfully.

"Anyone who is already exhausted at a young age or even suffers from sleep disorders and does not know how to deal with such pressures has worse conditions for successful learning," he said.

Skip next section Germany to order 4th new signals intelligence ship

Germany to order 4th new signals intelligence ship

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that Germany will acquire a fourth signals intelligence ship.

"These ships can hear and see what others cannot. They are our eyes and ears at sea. They perceive and analyze a vast range of signals and sounds," the minister said during a keel-laying ceremony for the third ship of this type to be built by the German company Rheinmetall.

The acquisition is part of a budget proposal that is pending parliamentary approval, he added.

Pistorius also said the ships were essential for providing situational awareness and enabling precise maneuvering in times of increasing insecurity.

The new class of ships are expected to be delivered to the German Navy from 2029.

Skip next section Germany sees slowing economic momentum in 3rd quarter

Germany sees slowing economic momentum in 3rd quarter

The German Ministry of Economy says the country is experiencing an economic slowdown at the beginning of the third quarter.

"The economic boom in energy-intensive industries, which was driven by increased foreign demand in the wake of the conflict in the Middle East, appears to be slowing down," the ministry said in its monthly report.

High energy costs have caused domestic consumption to decline considerably, a trend also driven by the conflict, the report said.

Skip next section Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia

Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia

German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said.

She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.

Read more about this story here.

Skip next section Germany's homeownership rate falls to 20-year low

Germany's homeownership rate falls to 20-year low

Fewer people in Germany are living in homes they own, with the country's homeownership rate falling to its lowest level in 20 years, according to a study.

The rate now stands at 43.5%, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported, citing research by the Pestel Institute.

Institute director Matthias Günther said Germany ranked last in Europe for homeownership.

Günther pointed to high construction costs, higher interest rates and housing policy over recent years.

"Even where property prices are stagnating or falling, even dual-income households on average salaries are barely able to afford a home of their own," he said.

According to the study, residential construction costs have risen by 160% since 2000, compared with a 64% increase in overall consumer prices.

Younger people are bearing much of the impact, Günther said. Almost three-quarters of people aged 25 to 45 currently live in rented accommodation, the study found.

Skip next section Germany and Hungary seek reset after political change

Germany and Hungary seek reset after political change

Germany and Hungary have "an enormous amount of catching up to do" in their diplomatic relations, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said.

The politician is visiting Hungary as the first German foreign minister to do so in almost seven years.

"Hungary and Germany are opening a new chapter together," Wadephul said before his departure.

He said the political change in Hungary offered an opportunity to rebuild relations "at great speed" on a foundation of mutual trust and reliability.

Hungary's new government had launched important reforms within a short period, he said, adding that a return to the rule of law and implementation of EU requirements were good news both for Europe and for Hungarians.

The nationalist Fidesz party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. Orban had faced years of criticism from the EU over concerns about democracy and the rule of law.

Since May, conservative Prime Minister Peter Magyar has led a new pro-European government.

Wadephul said predictable rules and the rule of law were important not only for public confidence but also for companies considering investment.

"If fair and reliable competitive conditions once again apply to companies from all EU member states, Hungary's economy will benefit considerably," he said.

German companies already account for around 250,000 jobs in Hungary, according to Wadephul.

A delegation of German business representatives is accompanying him to Budapest to discuss what further steps are needed.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn.

Germany is looking for a fresh start with Hungary after years of strained relations.

Relations had been difficult under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, whose nationalist Fidesz party faced years of criticism from the European Union over democracy and the rule of law.

In other news, fewer people in Germany are living in homes they own, according to research, with the country now ranking last in Europe for homeownership.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: India women's team refuse Asia Cup cricket trophy from Pakistan minister
entries.summary: India's women's cricket team skipped the trophy presentation with Pakistani minister Mohsin Naqvi after beating Sri Lanka to win a record eighth Asia Cup title. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India's women cricketers refuse cup from Pakistan minister

Published September 14, 2026last updated September 14, 2026

India's women's cricket team skipped the trophy presentation with Pakistani minister Mohsin Naqvi after beating Sri Lanka to win a record eighth Asia Cup title. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • India beat Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai on Sunday
  • The team skipped the trophy presentation with Mohsin Naqvi, Pakistan's interior minister
  • China reduced forces along India border last year, says Defense Ministry report

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Monday, September 14:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. 

Skip next section CJP supports 10-year ban on lawmakers who defect parties for money

CJP supports 10-year ban on lawmakers who defect parties for money

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Monday threw its support behind senior lawyer and former Congress minister Kapil Sibal's call for a 10-year ban on lawmakers who defect from one political party to another after being elected, if the defection is carried out for money or under pressure.

Saurav Das, CJP co-convenor, said this aligned with CJP's first demand charter released by founder Abhijeet Dipke, which called for a much stricter punishment of a 20-year ban from "holding any public office and contesting elections."

According to Das, political defections, including allegedly bribing lawmakers with large sums of money to topple elected governments "is a fraud committed on the country."

"Such fraud should never happen," Das wrote on X.

Das also called for reform of India's anti-defection law, arguing that it is outdated and has been misused by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Skip next section WATCH: How India has become Russia's trade lifeline

WATCH: How India has become Russia's trade lifeline

The war in Ukraine reshaped trade between India and Russia. Oil still dominates, but Indian companies are gaining ground in a wider range of sectors.

Skip next section After devastating floods, India approves electricity exports to Nepal till December

After devastating floods, India approves electricity exports to Nepal till December

India has approved electricity exports to Nepal for up to 18 hours a day until December 31, after devastating floods destroyed more than 12 hydropower plants and wiped out about a tenth of the neighboring country's generation capacity.

"The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period ​and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal," India's Power Ministry said on Monday.

The floods, triggered by a glacier collapse, killed nearly 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet, while more than 5,300 people, including about 900 hydropower workers, remain missing.

Almost all of Nepal's electricity is supplied by hydropower plants. Following the floods, Nepal has stopped electricity exports and said it would import power from India to cover shortages.

Skip next section China reduced forces along India border last year, says Defense Ministry report

China reduced forces along India border last year, says Defense Ministry report

India said the deployment of Chinese forces along the northern border fell significantly in 2025, as increased diplomatic engagements between India and China contributed to greater stability along the disputed border.

The annual report of the Ministry of Defense said Indian Army deployments across all sectors of the Line of Actual Control (LAC) remained "robust," even as about 10 Chinese combined-arms brigade-sized formations remained deployed along the LAC.

The thaw in ties came as Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Tianjin in August last year, while a senior military-level meeting between Beijing and New Delhi was held in October, the report said.

Meanwhile, the report also said the security situation in Jammu and Kashmir remained "firmly under control," with violence, protests and stone-pelting incidents declining, according to the ministry.

The report also mentioned the military conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbors India and Pakistan last year, saying that New Delhi has undertaken a comprehensive review of military capability gaps, with a focus on "force restructuring, enhancing jointness and integrating emerging technologies."

Skip next section Asia Cup win ends with India trophy snub of Pakistan minister

Asia Cup win ends with India trophy snub of Pakistan minister

Once again, political acrimony between India and Pakistan spilled out onto the cricket field as India's women's team refused to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) president Mohsin Naqvi, who also happens to be Pakistan's interior minister.

The incident is a stark replay of the Asia Cup controversy from last year, when India's men's team also skipped the prize ceremony with Naqvi after defeating archrival Pakistan in the Asia Cup finals.

On Sunday, India beat Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai, winning a record-extending eight continental titles.

However, the team did not attend the trophy presentation with Naqvi, also the chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board.

The ceremony was delayed by nearly an hour before ending abruptly after Naqvi presented the runners-up medals to the Sri Lankan team.

Indian officials instead conducted their own medal presentation for the champions.

"That stand has been taken by BCCI (India's cricket board) and we stand by it," India coach Amol Muzumdar told reporters. "For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough."

India and Pakistan, who last year engaged in a military conflict that threatened to turn into a full-blown war, avoid bilateral cricket series and only meet in international tournaments.

On Sunday, India dominated the final after scoring 183-5, with Smriti Mandhana scoring 59 and Shafali Verma 68. Spinner Shree Charani then took 4-20 as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 111.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello!

This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi studio, bringing you the top headlines from across India.

Stop me if you've heard this before — an Indian cricket team wins a cup and refuses to accept it from the Asian Cricket Council's chief, Mohsin Naqvi, who also happens to be Pakistan's interior minister.

This happened with India's women's cricket team after they won the Asia Cup on Sunday.

The exact same scenario played out last year following India's victory over Pakistan in the men's Asia Cup final, when the Indian team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the border, according to a statement by India's Ministry of Defense, China significantly reduced its troop presence along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with India last year, as Beijing and New Delhi continue their diplomatic engagement.

For all this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: Pay to ghost your boss: Japan's resignation business
entries.summary: Resignation agencies in Japan help employees leave their jobs seamlessly in just 15 minutes. Young people are especially eager to use their services.
entries.content:
September 14, 2026

Resignation agencies in Japan help employees leave their jobs seamlessly in just 15 minutes. Young people are especially eager to use their services.

For Y.M., a Japanese man in his early 20s, his first job out of university at a real estate sales firm quickly turned into a daily trial of endurance. Among his colleagues, he was always the one being screamed at.

According to his testimony featured on the website of Leadbrain, a Tokyo-based labor and human resources consulting firm, he sought a quiet way out because he was wary of how colleagues perceived him. He was reluctant to burden his parents and determined to avoid workplace conflict, which is a common attitude among working Japanese.

Rather than submitting his resignation in person, he opened his phone and began searching for a resignation proxy service, a third-party agency that could help him quit without direct interaction with his employer.

In Japan, vanishing from a workplace without notice is known as bakkure, a concept somewhat parallel to "ghosting" in modern dating. For many foreigners, leaving a job without notice would be considered an irresponsible and hurtful act. But within the logic of Japanese social interactions, vanishing is a way to avoid direct conflict and maintain harmony — at least on the outside.

Pay to flee

Demand for these resignation agencies is booming. Albatross, one of Japan's leading businesses of this kind, helps about 450 people quit without confrontation every month. They charge roughly €120 ($138.5) per client working a full-time job. The majority of these clients are young professionals in the service industry and manufacturing. The process can be completed within 15 minutes.

"The reasons why people requested us to resign for them range from physical violence to sexual harassment," said Yuka Hamada, the CEO of Albatross. "They are vulnerable in this case, and they are not brave enough to quit their job."

Around one in three people reported experiencing some form of harassment at work, according to a survey of Japanese workers aged 20 to 49 by consulting firm Shikigaku.

Harmony above all else

Traditional Japanese corporate culture originated during the post-World War II economic boom and relies heavily on the "lifetime employment" system. In this culture, loyalty is regarded as the highest virtue, and bosses often view resignations as insults, so many young employees fear resigning in person. 

"Announcing one's intention to resign can feel not merely like ending a contract, but like disappointing others or betraying expectations that one has previously continued to meet," said Hiroki Nakamori, an associate professor at Rikkyo University's Graduate School of Social Design Studies.

Japan is a non-confrontational culture, and people are expected to fall in line when making certain commitments to the company and its culture.

"Those who disturb the harmony are not appreciated, so someone leaving might feel they should just disappear without making too much of a fuss," said Hiroshi Ono, a professor of Human Resources Management at Hitotsubashi University Business School.

"Acting in a collective and acting in harmony is a sign of strength."

This cultural compulsion to avoid conflict runs deep. Even Japan's 17-Article Constitution, the 7th century foundation of modern Japanese governance, explicitly states: "Harmony should be valued and quarrels should be avoided."

Ghosting with consideration

But you can also politely ghost a job. "Clients may not say goodbye or express their gratitude directly to the company. In such cases, the agency can deliver these words on their behalf," says Albatross CEO Hamada.

It is the ultimate paradox of Japanese workplace culture: Even when ghosting, the employee feels compelled to abide by meiwaku — the social obligation to minimize trouble for others and preserve collective order above all else. This also applies to removing their personal items from the workplace.

"Even if a client intends to completely vanish from their job, we still advise them to clear off their desk" before leaving, added Hamada.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Israeli minister accuses 'NAZA' filmmakers of 'treason'
entries.summary: Israel's culture minister wants to strip the makers of a documentary on Israel's Gaza offensive of their citizenship. He accused the two of seeking "applause from antisemites around the world."
entries.content:
Israel

Israeli minister accuses 'NAZA' filmmakers of 'treason'

September 14, 2026

Israel's culture minister wants to strip the makers of a documentary on Israel's Gaza offensive of their citizenship. He accused the two of seeking "applause from antisemites around the world."

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar has threatened to strip filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of their citizenship after the two won a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival for a documentary about Israeli airstrikes killing Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

The film, called "NAZA" — a Hebrew acronym said to be used for counting the estimated number of civilians to be killed in a military strike — contains interviews with Israeli intelligence operatives behind the attacks.

Israel's military denies deliberately targeting civilians.

What did the culture minister and others say?

Zohar said Abraham and Szor were "willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world."

"I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state," Zohar wrote on X.

Far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir also used the platform for a post in which he called the two filmmakers "a disgrace and an embarrassment" to Israel.

The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, with the Supreme Court confirming in 2022 that the state may strip people of their nationality for acts of "disloyalty" such as espionage or treason.

What does the film 'NAZA' show?

For "NAZA," Abraham and Szor spoke to 24 Israeli military or intelligence personnel in nighttime interviews on rooftops in Tel Aviv.

Those interviewed gave details on the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza in Israel's offensive in retaliation for the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel.

According to figures by Gaza officials, which are considered to be broadly reliable by the UN, more than 73,000 Palestinian people, including 20,000 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks since the operation began.

Abraham said "the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanization of Palestinians."

The Israeli army has rejected allegations made in the 80-minute film, among other things criticizing the use of anonymous testimonies and saying the identities of the whistleblowers could not be verified.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy
entries.summary: European leaders are meeting over shipping, resources and security in the region amid pressure from the US, China and Russia. The EU sees the Arctic as key to its future security as melting ice makes it more accessible.
entries.content:
Europe

Finland: EU leaders meet to forge new Arctic policy

September 14, 2026

European leaders are meeting over shipping, resources and security in the region amid pressure from the US, China and Russia. The EU sees the Arctic as key to its future security as melting ice makes it more accessible.

European leaders are gathering in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Monday to plan a path forward for the bloc's presence in the Arctic.

The talks will focus on emerging shipping lanes, raw mineral deposits and security threats from the US, China and Russia.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, the prime ministers of Estonia and Latvia, the presidents of Lithuania and Romania, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and EU Council President Antonio Costa are all scheduled to attend Monday's "European Arctic Summit."

"The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," according to Tuomas Tikkanen — Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's senior adviser on European affairs.

Orpo, who initiated the summit, has emphasized that the Arctic is an, "increasingly important part of Europe's security environment."

Finland also insists European icebreaker capabilities are included in the strategy, saying they are key to Europe's ability to operate in the High North, adding that without them it would be impossible to protect supply and trade routes, or military presence across the region.

EU will use meeting to shape its new Arctic strategy

No formal decisions are expected Monday, but the European Commission has said the talks will help shape its new Arctic strategy, which will be unveiled over the next few weeks.

National leaders can still have a say impacting the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," said Finnish adviser Tikkanen.

The bloc's last strategy paper was released in 2021.

The Arctic, which is warming nearly four times faster than other regions, has seen increased activity as receding ice opens potential transport routes as well as access to mineral resources.

That changing environment has spurred the US, China and Russia to increase energy, resource and military activity.

In August, China and South Korea both sent container ships through the region, testing the viability of the North Sea Route in Russian territorial waters.

As Arctic ice melts, desire for control of the Arctic has heated up

Although Canada, China, Russia and Scandinavian countries are all considered Arctic nations, the most concerning development of late for the EU and member state Denmark have come from an entirely unexpected corner — the United States.

US President Donald Trump has threatened to blow up the NATO military alliance through his insistence that "the US must have Greenland" — a semi-autonomous island nation that is officially Danish territory — citing national security concerns, even threatening to take it by force if necessary.

Trump argues that Denmark cannot protect Greenland, which is not part of the EU, from China and Russia.

NATO has since launched a new security mission in the region.

Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, on a visit to Greenland, also announced closer cooperation and an investment package of €200 million ($231 million) to be used in part to set up infrastructure to extract valuable raw materials.

During her visit, von der Leyen vowed that the EU would "be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic," saying the package would "create new opportunities and a strong and engaged EU in both Greenland and the Arctic."

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: North Korea says recent drill shows 'huge destructive power'
entries.summary: North Korea carried out a coordinated live-fire exercise involving multiple weapons systems over the weekend. The drill came after the US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up five days of joint maritime exercises.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea says recent drill shows 'huge destructive power'

September 14, 2026

North Korea carried out a coordinated live-fire exercise involving multiple weapons systems over the weekend. The drill came after the US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up five days of joint maritime exercises.

North Korea said Monday that its recent "live-fire" drill demonstrated "huge destructive power."

During the test on Saturday, different types of weapons were fired simultaneously, with the aim of boosting the morale of North Korean troops and improving their capabilities to "completely collapse the enemy," according to the state news agency KCNA.

KCNA reported that the drill involved five army ​units and tested attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, tactical ballistic missiles, and other weapons systems.

Experts say North Korea is not slowing down its weapons activities, even after US President Donald Trump recently scaled back a military exercise with South Korea in an apparent effort to revive diplomacy with leader Kim Jong Un.

North Korea claims great military power

North Korean Marshal Pak Jong Chon was cited by KCNA as saying the drill intended to "improve the level of specialization to bring down the enemy's armed forces organizationally and structurally once an order is issued." He added that the mobilized weapons systems demonstrated "the huge destructive power of concentrated fire."

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said several missiles were fired on Saturday and traveled about 250 kilometers (155 miles) into North Korea's eastern waters.

The distances indicate that the weapons are designed to strike targets in South Korea, including US military bases.

North Korea's response to 'provocations'

The firing drill came a day after the United States, South Korea, and Japan concluded a trilateral military exercise that North Korea considers a provocation.

In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise conducted jointly with South Korea. According to the US president, the decision was due to his good relationship with Kim Jong Un.

North Korea rejected Trump's move, saying that shortening the exercise did not change its "provocative, aggressive nature."

The exercise ended six days earlier than originally scheduled.

Experts say Kim Jong Un likely believes his position in any potential diplomacy with the US has improved since his first meetings with Trump in 2018 and 2019. Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the US abandons its "hostile policy" toward his country and recognizes what he calls North Korea's status as a nuclear state.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
entries.summary: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade.
entries.content:
September 14, 2026

Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade.

Can land corridors offset the impact of the maritime blockade on Iran? The US-led maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports has severely disrupted trade through its southern ports, but it is also accelerating a strategy Tehran had discussed for years: moving more commerce through northern ports, railways and land corridors.

Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh, visiting Moscow for talks with Russian officials, said Iran should activate its northern borders and shift a significant share of imports and exports away from the country's southern maritime routes.

The idea is straightforward. Iran has seven land neighbors, access to the Caspian Sea and several routes linking it to Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and the Caucasus. In theory, that gives Tehran more options than a country dependent on a single maritime gateway.

The question is whether those routes have enough capacity to replace what is being lost at sea.

Northern routes offer room to expand

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, told DW that Iran does have unused capacity.

"Iran has more room to maneuver than its dependence on southern ports might suggest,” he said.

Iranian authorities said in late 2025 that the country's northern ports had more than 30 million tons of nominal annual capacity, with less than one-third in use. That suggests room for more grain, food and general cargo through the Caspian Sea.

Turkey provides another route toward Europe. Rail freight between Iran and Turkey depends partly on train ferries across Lake Van, which carried about 477,000 tons in 2024.

To the northeast, Sarakhs and Incheh Borun connect Iran through Turkmenistan toward Central Asia, Russia and potentially China. To the northwest, Astara is part of the International North-South Transport Corridor linking Iran to Azerbaijan and Russia, he said.

The Astara freight terminal is designed for 3.5 to 4 million tons a year, but handled only about 345,000 tons in the first five months of 2026. The unfinished Rasht-Astara rail link remains an important bottleneck.

For specific goods, these routes matter. Grain from Russia and Kazakhstan, medicines, industrial inputs and regional trade can be redirected more easily than crude oil.

Volume is the main obstacle

Jafar Ghaderi, a member of Iranian parliament's Economic Commission, recently said that 83% of what he described as Iran's 210 million tons of imports had traditionally moved through southern maritime borders, a tremendous volume of goods.

"Whenever we are under a maritime blockade, we face problems," hhe said. "How much capacity do our eastern, western and northern corridors actually have?"

The cost difference is also large. Majidreza Hariri, head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, said shipping one container from China to Iran through southern ports costs about $3,000 (€2,580), and that moving the same container overland costs roughly $12,000.

With around 2 million containers entering through the south annually, Hariri estimated that a prolonged shift to land routes could add about $18 billion to Iran's trading costs.

Salavati said the physical arithmetic helps explain why.

A 50,000-ton shipload would require around 2,000 truck journeys if each lorry carried 25 tons. Those trucks would then be unavailable for domestic distribution, while longer journeys increase fuel, insurance, warehousing and border costs.

Low-value goods are particularly vulnerable because transport expenses account for a larger share of their final price.

Energy is much harder to reroute

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said Iranian officials are often discussing two different kinds of alternatives.

One involves alternative navigation lanes around Hormuz. The other involves shifting trade toward Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, the Caspian region, Jask and Chabahar.

Neither provides a full substitute for southern energy exports.

A large crude tanker can carry roughly 1.5 to 2 million barrels. Replicating that volume by road would require thousands of tanker trucks.

Rail is more efficient, but still cannot match the cost, speed or scale of maritime transport.

Pakistan can help move imports through Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Iraq can support regional trade and limited fuel flows. Caspian routes can connect Iran to Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.

But none can replace large-scale crude shipments to Asian buyers.

"So the plan is realistic as a resilience strategy, but not as a replacement strategy,” Shokri told DW.

Jask pipeline shows both potential and limits

The Goreh-Jask pipeline was built specifically to reduce Iran's dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by moving crude to the Gulf of Oman.

That gives Jask greater strategic importance than most overland corridors.

But Shokri says actual usable capacity has remained far below the project's original ambition.

The lesson is broader: building a pipeline is not the same as creating a functioning export system. Storage, terminals, buyers, insurance, security and financial settlement all have to work together.

Fixed infrastructure also creates new vulnerabilities during wartime.

A resilience strategy, not an escape route

Land corridors can help Iran keep essential economic activity alive.

They can move food, medicine, industrial inputs and some regional exports. They can also deepen Iran's economic links with Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq.

If investment continues, the blockade may accelerate infrastructure projects that Tehran had previously treated as long-term opportunities.

But these routes come with higher costs, limited capacity and their own political dependencies.

For Iran, that means the blockade could leave a lasting structural effect by pushing trade away from the south and making northern and overland connections more important.

It does not mean Iran can replace maritime trade.

The corridors can reduce vulnerability, distribute risk and buy time. They cannot reproduce the scale of the Persian Gulf ports and seaborne energy exports on which much of Iran's economy has long depended.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
entries.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.
entries.content:
Germany

In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners

September 14, 2026

A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.

Abdu Taviq, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Taviq is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.

"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to kindergartens and German courses, for example, affect me directly."

Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.

Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's upcoming election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, this will be a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Taviq is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.

Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Taviq decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.

Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.

That happens to be another one of Taviq's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.

More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Taviq, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: Canada seeks 'unique alliance' with EU, Carney says
entries.summary: Mark Carney clarified Canada's EU ambitions amid a WSJ report that Ottawa was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc.
entries.content:
Canada

Canada seeks 'unique alliance' with EU, Carney says

September 14, 2026

Mark Carney clarified Canada's EU ambitions amid a WSJ report that Ottawa was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday said he was pursuing unprecedented closeness with the European Union to reduce its dependence on its economically hostile neighbor, but not a membership with the bloc.

"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival.

"What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — is a unique ​alliance between Canada and the European Union," he said. "We share the same values, we have the same priorities and ​we have very complementary strengths."

Carney's clarification came after a report by the Wall Street Journal claimed he was exploring whether Canada could become an "associate member" of the bloc. The newspaper reported that the EU was open to the idea of granting Canada associate membership — a status it would have to create for the North American nation.

Carney's mission EU

The remarks precede the Canadian prime minister's scheduled trip to France this week.

In Strasbourg, France, Carney will become the first head of government to attend the "State of the European Union" address before delivering his own speech at the European Parliament.

His visit is a "tremendous symbol," said Tobias Cremer, a European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a March resolution calling for stronger EU-Canada cooperation.

"Canada has many of the resources that Europe is very much short of, whether it's in terms of energy, whether it's rare earths (and) raw minerals," Cremer said.

Canada is already the first non-EU Nation to join the bloc's defense procurement program, while Carney was involved in Canada joining the Eurovision Song Contest for 2027.

Meanwhile, Montreal is set to host an EU-Canada summit where Carney said discussions will begin on building a "much stronger and deeper economic and security partnership."

Canada's increasing closeness with the EU comes when the country is in the middle of an escalating trade war with its largest trading partner and neighbor, the United States.
